newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Swiss banks set up $70million Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swiss banks set up $70million Holocaust fund.

text.p: Switzerland's three biggest banks, galvanised by international pressure, said on Wednesday they had created a 100 million Swiss franc ($70 million) Holocaust memorial fund as a gesture of good will towards their critics.

Seizing the initiative after months of public battering from Jewish groups, the three pillars of Swiss finance -- Union Bank of Switzerland, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp SBC -- invited the Swiss government and central bank to join the fund.
"Reflecting the intensive discussions which are under way in Switzerland to create such a fund, the...time has come for action, not words," the banks said in a joint statement.

Jewish groups have accused banks of hoarding the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and of stonewalling family members seeking to get back money that Jews stashed in neutral Switzerland to hide it from Adolf Hitler and the Nazis.
Swiss Jewish leaders hailed the move as a solid first step towards settling what has become an emotional debate and stirred latent anti-Semitism in Switzerland.
"We think this is a very positive step. There is now some movement in the whole affair, and that is good," said Thomas Lyssy, vice president of the Swiss Jewish Federation.
He said the size of the fund was not the important point, but rather the fact that Swiss banks had finally acted to address years of complaints from Jewish critics.
"We should not discuss sums but instead look at the initiative, which is very positive," he said.

Bankers said the contribution, already on deposit at the Swiss National Bank, underscored banks' willingness to come to grips with a problem that tarnished their image around the world and triggered threats by some Jewish leaders to call a boycott.

"The banks trust that this initiative will clear the way for the Swiss government, Switzerland's business and financial community and Jewish organisations to work together towards finding a just and equitable solution to the issues involved," the joint statement said.

"The fund is a humanitarian gesture and shows that the banks want to detach themselves from their formalistic attitude toward victims in the past," added Silvia Matile-Steiner, spokeswoman for the Swiss Bankers Association.

The banks said the special escrow account would form the basis for the "Humanitarian Fund for the Victims of the Holocaust" and was open for more contributions from others, including the government and the Swiss National Bank (SNB).

Berne and the SNB have said they would await findings of an panel of international historians investigating Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre -- including purchases of looted Nazi gold -- before deciding on contributions.

The banks' statement stressed the new fund had no bearing on current efforts under way to identify unclaimed assets belonging to victims of the Nazi regime. A panel agreed last May by Swiss bankers and Jewish groups is searching banks for any such funds.

The funds, contributed equally by all three big banks, will remain at the central bank for the time being until the Swiss government determines how the memorial fund will be structured, the statement said.
UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann said the size of the contribution was not determined by any specific calculation.
"You take a round number and 100 (million) is a nice figure. There is no calculation behind it, 100 is a round figure," she said.
